q: Which main criterion is used by the World Bank in classifying different countries?
o: Literacy rate
Per Capita Income (Average income)
Infant Mortality Rate
Total population
e: In World Development Reports brought out by the World Bank, Per Capita Income (total income divided by total population) is used as the main criterion.

q: What is the correct formula to calculate Per Capita Income?
o: Total population of the country / Total income of the country
Total income of the country / Total population of the country
Total exports / Total imports
Total tax revenue × Population
e: Per Capita Income (average income) is the total income of the country divided by its total population.

q: Among Haryana, Kerala, and Bihar, which state has the lowest per capita income?
o: Haryana
Kerala
Bihar
Punjab
e: According to NCERT data comparing Haryana, Kerala, and Bihar, Bihar has the lowest per capita income.

q: Which of the following states has the lowest Infant Mortality Rate (IMR) according to NCERT data?
o: Bihar
Haryana
Kerala
Jharkhand
e: Kerala has the lowest Infant Mortality Rate because it has adequate provision of basic health and educational facilities.

q: What does "Infant Mortality Rate (IMR)" measure?
o: The number of children who die before the age of one year as a proportion of 1,000 live children born in that particular year
Total number of children under age 5
Number of doctors per 100 residents
Total hospitals in a state
e: Infant Mortality Rate indicates the number of children dying before the age of one year per 1,000 live births in that year.

q: Which organisation publishes the Human Development Report (HDR)?
o: World Bank
United Nations Development Programme (UNDP)
International Monetary Fund (IMF)
World Trade Organisation (WTO)
e: The United Nations Development Programme (UNDP) publishes the Human Development Report comparing countries on educational levels, health status, and per capita income.

q: How is Body Mass Index (BMI) calculated?
o: Weight in kg divided by the square of height in metres
Height in metres divided by weight in kg
Weight in kg multiplied by age in years
Daily calorie intake divided by height
e: BMI is calculated by dividing a person’s weight in kilograms by the square of their height in metres.

q: If an adult’s Body Mass Index (BMI) is less than 18.5, how is the person classified?
o: Overweight
Undernourished
Obese
Athletically fit
e: A BMI of less than 18.5 indicates an adult is undernourished, whereas more than 25 indicates overweight.

q: Which neighbouring country ranks ahead of India in the Human Development Index (HDI) table given in NCERT?
o: Nepal
Sri Lanka
Pakistan
Myanmar
e: A smaller neighbouring country, Sri Lanka, ranks much ahead of India in the Human Development Index.

q: Which of the following is a renewable resource whose overuse has become a serious concern in India?
o: Crude oil
Coal
Groundwater
Bauxite
e: Groundwater is a renewable resource replenished by nature, yet overuse—especially in agriculture—has seriously depleted water levels in about one-third of India’s districts.

q: What defines "non-renewable resources"?
o: Are automatically replenished every monsoon
Will get exhausted after a few years of use because they have a fixed stock on Earth
Come strictly from solar radiation
Never run out regardless of usage
e: Non-renewable resources like crude oil and coal have a fixed stock on Earth that cannot be replenished in human timescales.

q: "We have not inherited the world from our forefathers — we have borrowed it from our children." This quote highlights which principle?
o: Sustainable Development
Unregulated industrialisation
Rapid resource exhaustion
Monoculture farming
e: This quote emphasises sustainability of development—using resources carefully so future generations’ needs are not compromised.

q: What is "Literacy Rate" defined as in NCERT?
o: The proportion of literate population in the 7-and-above age group
Percentage of university graduates only
Proportion of children aged 0–6 years
Percentage of salaried urban workers
e: Literacy Rate measures the proportion of literate population in the 7-and-above age group.

q: The Public Distribution System (PDS) is an example of what kind of developmental support?
o: Private luxury service
Public Facility
Foreign direct investment
Corporate subsidy
e: Services provided collectively by government such as PDS ration shops, government schools, and hospitals are Public Facilities.

q: What is "Net Attendance Ratio"?
o: Total number of children of age group 14 and 15 years attending school as a percentage of total number of children in the same age group
Attendance of MPs in Parliament
Daily attendance of factory workers
Number of university professors
e: Net Attendance Ratio is the total number of children aged 14–15 attending school as a percentage of total children in that age group.

q: Economic activities based directly on natural resources—such as agriculture, dairy, fishing, and forestry—belong to which sector?
o: Primary Sector
Secondary Sector
Tertiary Sector
Quaternary Sector
e: Activities producing goods by directly exploiting natural resources belong to the Primary Sector (also called agriculture and related sector).

q: Which economic sector is also known as the "Industrial Sector"?
o: Primary Sector
Secondary Sector
Tertiary Sector
Unorganised Sector
e: Because the Secondary Sector transforms natural products through manufacturing processes into finished goods, it is also called the Industrial Sector.

q: Transport, storage, communication, banking, and trade belong to which sector of the economy?
o: Primary Sector
Secondary Sector
Tertiary Sector (Service Sector)
Only Public Sector
e: Activities that generate services rather than physical goods fall under the Tertiary Sector, also called the Service Sector.

q: What is "Gross Domestic Product (GDP)"?
o: The sum of the value of all final goods and services produced within a country during a particular year across all three sectors
Total value of foreign imports
Total weight of agricultural crops only
Sum of civil service salaries only
e: GDP is the total market value of all final goods and services produced within a country during a particular year.

q: While calculating GDP, why is ONLY the value of "final goods and services" counted?
o: Because the value of final goods already includes the value of all intermediate goods used in making them, avoiding double counting
Because intermediate goods have zero price
Because wheat farmers never sell produce
Because only finished biscuits exist in markets
e: Final goods’ value already incorporates intermediate goods (e.g. wheat and flour inside biscuits), so counting intermediate goods separately would cause double counting.

q: In India today, which sector has the largest share in GDP, and which sector continues to be the largest employer?
o: Largest share in GDP: Tertiary sector; Largest employer: Primary sector
Largest share in GDP: Primary sector; Largest employer: Tertiary sector
Both GDP and employment: Secondary sector
All three sectors hold identical shares
e: The Tertiary sector became the largest producing sector in India’s GDP, yet the Primary sector still accounts for the largest share of employment.

q: What is "Disguised unemployment" (underemployment)?
o: A situation where more people are employed in a task (especially farming) than required, so removing a few does not reduce total production
When workers earn large bonuses
When factories operate 24 hours
When a worker is openly idle without any task
e: Underemployment/disguised unemployment occurs when people are apparently working, yet all are made to work less than their potential—like extra family hands on a tiny farm.

q: Under the Mahatma Gandhi National Rural Employment Guarantee Act (MGNREGA), 2005, how many days of guaranteed wage employment per year are promised to rural households?
o: 50 days
100 days
150 days
365 days
e: MGNREGA 2005 guarantees 100 days of wage employment in a year to all those able and in need of work in rural areas.

q: Under MGNREGA 2005, what happens if the government fails in its duty to provide employment within the stipulated period?
o: It gives unemployment allowances to the people
The applicant is permanently barred
A penalty is charged from the family
The village Panchayat is dissolved
e: If the government fails in its duty to provide employment under MGNREGA, it will give unemployment allowances to the applicants.

q: Which sector covers enterprises registered by the government, following labour laws (Factories Act, Minimum Wages Act) and offering regular terms of employment?
o: Unorganised sector
Organised sector
Disguised sector
Informal sector
e: The Organised Sector consists of government-registered enterprises following official laws, offering fixed hours, paid leave, and job security.

q: Which of the following is a characteristic of the "Unorganised Sector"?
o: Guaranteed paid leave and retirement pension
Small and scattered units largely outside government control, low/irregular wages, no paid leave, and lack of job security
Strict 8-hour day with double overtime pay
Formal appointment letters for all staff
e: The unorganised sector comprises small, scattered units outside effective government regulation, offering low, irregular pay and no job security or paid leave.

q: On the basis of ownership of assets and delivery of services, sectors of the economy are classified into—
o: Public Sector and Private Sector
Primary and Tertiary Sectors
Urban and Rural Sectors
Export and Import Sectors
e: Based on ownership of assets and responsibility for services, economic activities are divided into Public Sector and Private Sector.

q: Which pair consists purely of Public Sector enterprises in India?
o: TISCO and Reliance Industries Limited
Indian Railways and Post Office
Infosys and Wipro
Ashok Leyland and Hero MotoCorp
e: Indian Railways and Post Office are owned and operated by the government (Public Sector), whereas TISCO and Reliance are privately owned.

q: What is the primary motive guiding the activities of the Private Sector?
o: Free charitable service only
To earn profits
Collecting income taxes
Distributing goods free of cost
e: Private sector enterprises are owned by private individuals or companies and are primarily guided by the motive to earn profits.

q: Making cloth from cotton or sugar from sugarcane belongs to which sector?
o: Primary Sector
Secondary Sector
Tertiary Sector
Non-economic activity
e: Manufacturing finished cloth from cotton or sugar from sugarcane takes place in the Secondary (Industrial) Sector.

q: Which example clearly illustrates that what may be development for one may even be destructive for another?
o: Industrialists wanting large dams for more electricity may displace tribals and submerge their ancestral lands
Providing clean drinking water to every village
Opening libraries in government schools
Installing solar street lights
e: Building large dams benefits industrialists with electricity while submerging the lands and livelihoods of displaced tribal communities.

q: Apart from higher income, what non-material things do people commonly seek in life as developmental goals?
o: Equal treatment, freedom, security, and respect from others
Only gold and silver ornaments
Only luxurious mansions
Only imported automobiles
e: Besides income, people seek equal treatment, freedom, security, and respect—showing people look at a mix of goals for development.

q: "Money in your pocket cannot buy all the goods and services that you may need to live well." Which of the following cannot normally be purchased solely by an individual’s money?
o: A pollution-free environment, collective protection from infectious diseases, and a safe community
Television sets and refrigerators
Clothes and shoes
Private cars and furniture
e: Money cannot individually buy a pollution-free environment or protect you from infectious diseases unless the whole community takes preventive steps.

q: What is a major limitation of using "Average Income" (Per Capita Income) to compare development across countries?
o: Average income hides disparities—it does not show how income is distributed among the people
Average income always equals zero
Population is ignored in computing averages
Average income counts only agriculture
e: Just like Countries A and B in NCERT, two countries can share the same average income even when one has equitable distribution and another has extreme inequality.

q: Why does Kerala rank better than Haryana on human development indicators despite having a lower per capita income?
o: Because Kerala has adequate provision of basic health and educational facilities (public facilities), yielding very low IMR and high literacy
Because Kerala has zero factories
Because Haryana has no schools
Because Kerala has a population of only 1 lakh
e: Because of strong public facilities like PDS, primary healthcare, and education, Kerala records much lower IMR and higher literacy than Haryana.

q: According to the World Development Report (2019 edition cited in NCERT), India fell into which income category of countries?
o: High income (Rich) countries
Low middle income countries
Extremely low income countries
High-income OECD countries
e: In the World Development Report data cited in NCERT, India came in the category of "low middle income countries" (below high-income threshold of US$ 49,300).

q: Which THREE indicators does the UNDP use in the Human Development Index (HDI) to compare countries?
o: Educational levels of the people, health status (Life Expectancy at birth), and per capita income
Military budget, nuclear arsenal, and population density
Per capita income, gold reserves, and highway length
Forest cover, coal stock, and annual rainfall
e: UNDP’s Human Development Report compares countries based on educational levels, health status (life expectancy at birth), and per capita income.

q: What does "Life Expectancy at birth" denote?
o: Average expected length of life of a person at the time of birth
Minimum retirement age
Age of school admission
Minimum voting age
e: Life Expectancy at birth denotes the average expected length of life of a person at the time of birth.

q: In which regions of India is groundwater overuse particularly severe according to NCERT?
o: Agriculturally prosperous regions of Punjab and Western U.P., hard rock plateau areas of central and south India, some coastal areas and rapidly growing urban settlements
Only Himalayan glaciers
Only Andaman & Nicobar Islands
Only Ladakh cold desert
e: Groundwater overuse is particularly found in Punjab, Western UP, central/south Indian plateau areas, and fast-growing urban settlements.

q: According to the world crude oil reserves table in NCERT, at the current rate of extraction, the world’s total reserves would last for roughly how many years?
o: About 10 years
About 50 years
About 500 years
Forever without depletion
e: NCERT’s world reserves table indicates global crude oil stocks would last roughly 47–50 years if extraction continues at the present pace.

q: What is the impact of rising crude oil prices on an oil-importing country like India?
o: The import bill rises and higher fuel/transport costs become a burden for everyone in the economy
India’s oil exports double immediately
Petrol becomes automatically cheaper
It causes zero economic effect
e: India depends heavily on oil imports; therefore rising crude oil prices sharply raise costs and become a burden for everyone.

q: Which is the most likely developmental goal for a landless rural labourer?
o: More days of work and better wages, local school offering quality education for children, and no social discrimination
Expansion of international airports
Investing in foreign stock exchanges
Lower export tariffs on tractors
e: A landless rural labourer seeks more days of work, better wages, quality local schooling for children, and dignity without discrimination.

q: Why is providing services collectively through Public Facilities cheaper and better than buying them individually?
o: Because organising collective security for an entire locality or running one school for village children is far cheaper and feasible than hiring individual guards or tutors per house
Because public facilities cost zero rupees to build
Because private services are banned
Because only billionaires qualify for public facilities
e: Collectively providing security, schools, healthcare, and clean environments lowers per-capita costs dramatically and ensures universal access.

q: In which currency is Per Capita Income calculated for comparing all countries internationally?
o: Indian Rupees (INR)
US Dollars ($)
Japanese Yen
Swiss Franc
e: Per capita income is calculated in US Dollars for all countries so that meaningful international comparisons can be made.

q: When a woman looks at not only pay but also job security, safe working environment, and time for family while choosing employment, what does this prove?
o: That for development and job choices, people consider a mix of goals—not just income, but also security, dignity, and working conditions
That wages play zero role in employment decisions
That distant locations are always preferred
That paid leave is illegal
e: A job with slightly lower pay but regular security, dignity, and learning opportunities is often preferred—showing development involves a mix of goals.

q: Which example best illustrates the interdependence among Primary, Secondary, and Tertiary sectors?
o: Farmers grow sugarcane (Primary) -> sugar mills process it into sugar (Secondary) -> transport, banking, and traders distribute sugar (Tertiary)
Farmers burn all produce without markets
Banks cultivate wheat inside vaults
Steel mills operate without iron ore or transport
e: Primary provides raw materials, Secondary manufactures finished goods, and Tertiary provides transport, storage, finance, and trade—making all three interdependent.

q: Which factor explains the rapid rise in importance of the Tertiary Sector in India over the past 40–50 years?
o: Rising demand for basic services (hospitals, schools, banks), growth of agriculture/industry boosting transport/trade, rising incomes fuelling tourism/private education, and growth of IT services
Complete closure of all Indian farms and factories
Abolition of transport and trade
Ban on communication technologies
e: NCERT gives four reasons: expansion of basic services, development of primary/secondary boosting transport/trade, rising incomes increasing leisure/private services, and emergence of IT-based services.

q: Do all workers in India’s Tertiary (Service) Sector earn high incomes?
o: Yes, everyone earns high corporate salaries
No; while one end employs skilled IT and banking professionals, a very large number of shopkeepers, repair persons, and transport workers barely manage a living
Poverty does not exist in the service sector
Only doctors belong to the tertiary sector
e: Only a limited part of the service sector provides high-paying skilled jobs; a huge number of small shopkeepers, repair persons, and transport workers earn meagre incomes.

q: Why does agriculture (Primary sector) still employ the largest share of workers in India even though its share in GDP has fallen sharply?
o: Because not enough jobs were created in the secondary and tertiary sectors to absorb the surplus labour from agriculture
Because factories banned hiring Indian workers
Because farming pays higher wages than IT
Because cities prohibit rural migration
e: While industrial and service output rose sharply, employment generation in secondary and tertiary sectors did not keep pace, leaving half of workers in low-productivity farming.

q: In Laxmi’s farm example (2 hectares of unirrigated land with 5 family members), how does building a well or canal irrigation create additional employment?
o: The family can cultivate a second crop (like wheat during rabi), creating extra work in sowing, watering, weeding, and harvesting, while dam/canal construction generates jobs
Farming stops during the monsoon
The family loses land ownership
Crop yield drops to zero
e: Irrigation enables taking a second rabi crop on the same land, absorbing disguised labour productively while canal/dam construction creates further rural jobs.

q: According to a study by the Planning Commission / NITI Aayog cited in NCERT, roughly 20 lakh jobs can be created in which single sector alone?
o: Education sector
Space tourism
Cricket industry
Mobile imports
e: Planning Commission (now NITI Aayog) estimated that nearly 20 lakh jobs can be created in the education sector alone (and over 35 lakh in tourism).

q: According to the Planning Commission / NITI Aayog estimate in NCERT, how many additional jobs per year can be generated if tourism is improved?
o: More than 5 lakh
More than 10 lakh
More than 35 lakh
More than 1 crore
e: If tourism as a sector is improved, more than 35 lakh additional jobs can be generated every year.

q: What type of works are given preference under MGNREGA (2005)?
o: Works that help increase production from land in the future (such as water conservation, ponds, canals, and rural infrastructure)
Building luxury shopping malls in metro cities
Constructing international airports
Running software offices
e: MGNREGA gives preference to types of work that will help increase production from land in the future, creating durable rural assets.

q: Who are the main vulnerable workers requiring protection in the Unorganised Sector in rural and urban areas?
o: Rural: landless agricultural labourers, small/marginal farmers, sharecroppers, artisans; Urban: workers in small-scale industry, casual construction/trade/transport workers, street vendors, ragpickers
Only IAS officers and bank managers
Only MNC CEOs
Only MPs and Ministers
e: Rural landless/small farmers and artisans, along with urban casual construction, transport, street vendors, and SC/ST/backward-community workers, form the bulk of vulnerable unorganised workers.

q: Roughly what percentage of rural households in India consist of small and marginal farmers who need timely support of seeds, credit, and marketing?
o: About 20%
About 45%
About 80%
About 10%
e: According to NCERT, nearly 80% of rural households in India are in the small and marginal farmer category.

q: Why must the Public Sector (government) provide essential infrastructure like roads, bridges, railways, electricity, and irrigation dams?
o: Because these require huge capital investment beyond the capacity of the private sector, and private firms would charge high fees beyond poor people’s reach
Because private engineers cannot build bridges
Because nobody uses railways
Because private firms are banned from construction
e: Large-scale infrastructure requires massive spending and long payback periods; government undertakes it to keep essential services affordable and accessible for everyone.

q: The government buys wheat and rice from farmers at a "fair price", stores it in godowns, and sells it at lower prices through ration shops. What does this exemplify?
o: Government supporting both farmers (producers) and poor consumers simultaneously as part of its welfare responsibility
Private sector profit maximisation
International dumping
Disguised unemployment
e: In this way, the government bears part of the cost to simultaneously support farmers and poor consumers through Public Distribution.

q: Why do some formal enterprises secretly adopt unorganised-sector practices (hiring informally without benefits)?
o: To evade taxes and refuse to follow laws that protect labourers, thereby cutting costs and raising profits
Because workers dislike paid holidays
Because the government forbids formal contracts
Because provident fund accounts were abolished
e: Many enterprises adopt unorganised strategies to evade taxes and refuse compliance with labour-protection laws, forcing workers into low-paid, insecure jobs.

q: In the history of developed countries, in what sequence did dominance shift across the three sectors?
o: Primary Sector -> Secondary Sector -> Tertiary Sector
Tertiary -> Primary -> Secondary
Secondary -> Primary -> Tertiary
No shift occurred in any sector
e: Initially Primary dominated; then industrialisation shifted prominence to the Secondary sector; in the past century, the Tertiary sector became the largest in developed nations.

q: A farmer sells wheat to a flour mill, which sells flour to a biscuit company, which sells packets of biscuits to consumers. What category do the biscuits fall under?
o: Intermediate good
Final Good
Raw natural resource
Informal service
e: Biscuits reach the final consumer directly and are Final Goods, whereas wheat and flour used to make them are intermediate goods.

q: Countries A and B both have 5 citizens and identical average income of Rs 10,000. In Country A, all earn between Rs 9,500 and Rs 10,500; in Country B, four earn Rs 500 each and one earns Rs 48,000. What does this prove?
o: Most people prefer Country A; this proves that along with average income, equitable distribution of income matters greatly
Everyone prefers Country B regardless of personal income
Living standards in both countries are identical
Average income is always useless
e: Even with identical averages, Country A offers equitable distribution whereas Country B leaves 80% of citizens in extreme poverty.

q: Kerala has lower per capita income than Haryana, yet performs better on infant mortality and literacy. What key development lesson emerges from this?
o: High per capita income alone is insufficient; collective public investment in basic healthcare, schooling, and PDS is crucial for human development
High per capita income automatically worsens literacy
Haryana must shut down all industries
Healthcare has no impact on mortality
e: Money alone cannot buy collective public goods; strong public facilities in health, education, and PDS drive superior human development outcomes.

q: A person weighs 45 kg and is 1.5 metres tall. What is their BMI and nutritional classification?
o: BMI = 20.0 (Normal / well-nourished range, between 18.5 and 25)
BMI = 15.0 (Undernourished)
BMI = 30.0 (Overweight)
BMI = 22.5 (Undernourished)
e: BMI = 45 / (1.5 × 1.5) = 45 / 2.25 = 20.0, which lies between 18.5 and 25 (normal/healthy range).

q: Calculate the BMI of an adult weighing 40 kg with a height of 1.6 metres, and identify their status:
o: BMI ≈ 15.6 (Undernourished, since it is below 18.5)
BMI = 25.0 (Overweight)
BMI = 19.2 (Normal)
BMI = 28.0 (Obese)
e: BMI = 40 / (1.6 × 1.6) = 40 / 2.56 ≈ 15.63, which is below 18.5 and thus classified as undernourished.

q: Even though groundwater is a renewable resource, when does it face serious depletion?
o: When we extract and use groundwater faster than nature replenishes it through rainfall
When rivers stay flooded throughout the year
When all tubewells are shut off
When farmers rely solely on rainwater
e: If we use a renewable resource like groundwater more than what is being replenished by rain, it becomes overused and depleted.

q: Why is environmental degradation and sustainability of development not merely a national or state-level issue?
o: Because consequences of environmental degradation do not respect national or state boundaries; our ecological future is linked together
Because pollution remains strictly inside rich countries
Because crude oil never crosses borders
Because climate affects only oceans
e: Consequences of environmental degradation do not respect national or state boundaries; sustainability is a global concern because our future is linked together.

q: Compare the World Bank’s classification criterion with UNDP’s Human Development Report criterion. What is the fundamental difference?
o: World Bank relies solely on Per Capita Income, whereas UNDP combines educational levels and health status with per capita income
World Bank measures only literacy while UNDP measures only GDP
Both use identical single-variable formulas
UNDP ranks countries strictly by crude oil stocks
e: World Bank uses Per Capita Income alone, whereas UNDP’s HDI evaluates holistic human well-being across health, education, and income.

q: Comparing the developmental goals of a girl from a rich urban family and an Adivasi farmer from Narmada Valley reveals what principle?
o: Different persons have different life situations and aspirations, so they hold different—and sometimes conflicting—notions of development
Everyone on Earth holds identical developmental goals
Rural farmers have no aspirations
Urban youth seek only large irrigation dams
e: Different individuals have different developmental goals depending on their life situations—an urban girl may desire equal freedom and study abroad, while a rural farmer seeks fair prices and irrigation.

q: A district opens an expensive private luxury clinic while government primary health centres remain shut. Why will the district’s Infant Mortality Rate (IMR) likely remain high?
o: Because poor and ordinary families cannot afford expensive private care; lowering IMR requires accessible, affordable public healthcare facilities for all
Because private clinics lack doctors
Because schools alone prevent infant deaths
Because IMR does not depend on healthcare
e: Without affordable public health centres, most families lack timely maternal care and immunisation, keeping IMR high.

q: What is the core challenge in deciding "National Development" when a policy benefits one section while harming another?
o: Deciding whether there is a better, fair, and just path and whether the idea benefits a large number of people or only a small group
Automatically favouring the richest 1% without debate
Removing voting rights of affected residents
Banning public debate on projects
e: Thinking about national development requires asking whether there is a fair and just way of doing things and whether the idea benefits a large majority or only a small group.

q: How does promoting solar energy, wind energy, and rainwater harvesting directly support sustainability of development?
o: They reduce dependence on exhaustible non-renewable fossil fuels (coal, crude oil) and aid natural replenishment of renewable water resources
They double coal consumption
They rapidly drain aquifers
They increase carbon emissions tenfold
e: Non-renewable fossil fuels are finite; shifting to renewables and rainwater harvesting preserves resources and ecology for future generations.

q: In the state-wise NCERT table, what does Kerala’s high "Net Attendance Ratio" (for age 14–15) indicate?
o: A very high proportion of adolescents aged 14–15 actually continue attending secondary school instead of dropping out early
Only children under age 6 attend school
There are no higher schools
Schools operate one day a week
e: A high Net Attendance Ratio indicates most 14–15 year-olds stay in school rather than dropping out into early labour, unlike states with low attendance ratios.

q: Which combination best reflects indicators of "quality of life" beyond monetary income?
o: Life expectancy, Infant Mortality Rate, literacy rate, clean environment, and social security
Gold imports, stock prices, and luxury car sales only
Crude oil exports only
Currency printing volume only
e: Health (life expectancy, IMR), education (literacy, school attendance), clean air/water, and equality capture true quality of life.

q: In the NCERT crude oil reserves table, which region holds the largest reserves, and which major consuming country listed has reserves lasting the shortest time (~10.5 years)?
o: Largest reserves: Middle East (~70 years); Shortest domestic stock among listed entries: United States of America (~10.5 years)
Largest: USA; Shortest: Middle East
Largest: India; Shortest: Saudi Arabia
Every region holds equal 100-year stocks
e: As shown in NCERT’s table, the Middle East holds reserves lasting ~70 years while the USA’s own reserves would last only about 10.5 years at current extraction.

q: A worker chooses a Rs 35,000 regular, secure job with paid leave and time for family over a Rs 40,000 insecure job with no leave. What developmental truth does this illustrate?
o: People weigh a mix of developmental goals—job security, family time, and dignity—rather than maximising money income alone
Workers prefer earning less without reason
Insecure jobs never pay higher cash
Paid leave violates labour policy
e: People value a combination of goals including job security, working environment, and family time over higher pay alone.

q: A farmer sells wheat at Rs 20/kg to a flour mill, which grinds and sells flour at Rs 25/kg to a biscuit company. Using sugar and oil, the company produces 4 packets of biscuits sold to consumers for Rs 80 total. What amount enters GDP?
o: Rs 80 only (the value of final biscuits), NOT 20 + 25 + 80 = Rs 125
Rs 125 (adding all three stages)
Rs 20 only (wheat)
Rs 45 (wheat + flour)
e: The Rs 80 final price of biscuits already includes the value of wheat (Rs 20) and flour (Rs 25); summing them all would cause double counting.

q:
Classify the following four activities in order (1 to 4):
1. Beekeeper collecting honey
2. Potter making clay pots in a workshop
3. Courier agent delivering parcels
4. Doctor treating patients at a hospital
o: 1-Primary, 2-Secondary, 3-Tertiary, 4-Tertiary
1-Secondary, 2-Primary, 3-Tertiary, 4-Primary
1-Primary, 2-Primary, 3-Secondary, 4-Tertiary
1-Tertiary, 2-Secondary, 3-Primary, 4-Secondary
e: Beekeeping uses biological processes directly (Primary), pottery manufactures finished pots (Secondary), while courier and medical care provide services (Tertiary).

q: Does underemployment (disguised unemployment) occur ONLY in rural agriculture? Identify an urban example given in NCERT:
o: No; in urban areas thousands of casual painters, plumbers, repair persons, and cart pullers spend the whole day searching for little work or earning far below potential
Yes, disguised unemployment exists strictly on farms
Only bank CEOs face disguised unemployment
Only industrial robots create underemployment
e: Underemployment also exists in other sectors—e.g., thousands of casual urban workers (painters, plumbers, pushcart sellers) spend whole days earning very little.

q: How can setting up agro-based units in semi-rural areas generate new non-farm employment?
o: Setting up dal mills, cold storages, honey collection centres, and food processing units absorbs surplus farm labour locally into processing and trade
It stops local farming completely
It forces all villagers into unemployment
It increases wastage of vegetables
e: Dal mills, cold storage facilities (allowing farmers to store produce for better prices), honey centres, and food processing units generate substantial local employment.

q: In NCERT’s comparison of Kanta (office worker) and Kamal (daily-wage shop helper), what key differences distinguish the Organised from the Unorganised Sector?
o: Kanta receives regular salary, appointment letter, paid leave, PF, and job security, whereas Kamal gets daily wages with no paid leave and can be dismissed anytime
Kamal receives higher pension than Kanta
Kanta works without holidays or appointment letter
Both receive identical statutory provident fund

That literacy in Bihar is 43%

Primary Sector only

q:

Human Development Report — UNDP (Health, Education, Income)
MGNREGA — 2005 (100 days guaranteed work)
State with lowest Infant Mortality Rate — Bihar
e: Kerala has the lowest Infant Mortality Rate among the three compared states; Bihar has the highest IMR and lowest per capita income.

q: A policymaker argues: "Since per capita income is rising, government can reduce spending on public schools and primary health centres." Which evidence from NCERT best refutes this?

Only rich people require literacy
Private hospitals always offer free universal care
Public schools reduce national GDP
e: Haryana vs Kerala proves that rising private income cannot substitute for strong collective public facilities in health, education, and PDS.

q: Consider an Adivasi farmer opposing a large dam, an industrialist seeking dam electricity, and an unemployed engineer seeking construction jobs. What TWO truths about development emerge here?

(1) Development depends solely on crude oil, and (2) cities lack goals
(1) Conflict never arises over dams
e: NCERT highlights two core conclusions: (1) different persons can have different developmental goals, and (2) what may be development for one may be destructive for another.

q: Green Revolution farming raised incomes in Punjab, yet groundwater tables in many districts have now fallen dangerously low. Which principle does this case warn about?

Higher crop yield never harms aquifers
Groundwater is infinite and unaffected by pumping
Farming must be halted nationwide
e: Overexploiting even renewable resources like groundwater faster than rainfall replenishes them undermines long-term sustainability of development.

q:

Eliminating all government planning
Depleting aquifers for rapid returns

q: Which of the following factors is NOT included when the World Bank classifies countries into "High Income" vs "Low Income" in its World Development Report?

Unregulated non-renewable depletion
Zero-development policy
Privatisation of all public schools
e: Sustainable development meets present needs responsibly while transitioning to renewables so future generations’ needs and environment are protected.

q: Country A has Rs 50,000 average income with extreme inequality and few public clinics; Country B has Rs 40,000 average income with 95% literacy, low IMR, and universal public healthcare. Which fares better on Human Development?
o: Country B, because equitable distribution and strong public facilities yield superior health, literacy, and overall human development
Country A, because higher average income outweighs everything
Both show zero development
Country A automatically achieves higher literacy
e: Mirroring the Haryana vs Kerala comparison, Country B ranks higher in human development due to strong public health, literacy, and equitable welfare.

q: What makes deciding the path of "National Development" fundamentally complex?
o: Reconciling diverse and conflicting aspirations of citizens to choose a fair, just path that benefits the majority while remaining environmentally sustainable
Because average income alone solves every conflict
Because all citizens share identical interests
Because fossil fuels are infinite
e: National development involves balancing conflicting group interests fairly, investing in public facilities, and ensuring long-term sustainability.

q:
Consider the following statements:
1. A large private IT company offering regular salary, PF, and paid leave belongs to BOTH the Private Sector and the Organised Sector.
2. Indian Railways and Post Office belong to BOTH the Public Sector and the Tertiary Sector.
3. No agricultural enterprise can ever fall within the Organised Sector.
Which statements are true?
o: 1 and 2 only
2 and 3 only
1 and 3 only
All 1, 2 and 3
e: Statements 1 and 2 are true; statement 3 is false because a registered plantation or agri-company following labour regulations belongs to both Primary and Organised sectors.

q: In a value chain: Farmer sells cotton for Rs 500 -> Spinning mill sells yarn for Rs 900 -> Textile mill sells cloth for Rs 1,400 -> Garment maker sells finished shirts to consumers for Rs 2,200. What total amount enters GDP?
e: Only final goods’ value (Rs 2,200) is counted—which equally matches the sum of value added at each stage (500 + 400 + 500 + 800 = Rs 2,200), avoiding double counting.

q: Which of the following is NOT one of the four NCERT reasons explaining the huge growth of the Tertiary Sector in India between 1973–74 and 2013–14?
o: Government responsibility for basic services like hospitals, schools, post, banks, and defence
Growth of agriculture and industry generating higher demand for transport, trade, and storage
Rising income levels driving demand for eating out, tourism, private clinics, plus growth of IT-based services
Legally shutting down all farming and manufacturing industries nationwide
e: On the contrary, growth in agriculture and industry directly stimulated demand for tertiary services like transport, trade, and storage.

q: Secondary and Tertiary sectors employ less than half of India’s workforce yet produce over four-fifths of total GDP. What does this imply about average worker productivity and income?
o: Average productivity and earnings per worker in the Primary (agriculture) sector are far lower than in Secondary and Tertiary sectors due to massive underemployment
Agricultural workers earn the highest per-worker income
The Tertiary sector produces zero output
Average output per worker is identical across all three sectors
e: When over half the workforce produces a minor slice of GDP, output and income per worker in farming are severely depressed by widespread underemployment.

q: How do MGNREGA (2005) and promoting rural cold storages/dal mills complement each other in solving rural unemployment?
o: MGNREGA provides immediate guaranteed short-term wage security (100 days) and rural assets, while cold storages and dal mills build year-round agro-industrial employment
Both shut down permanently after 100 days
Cold storages serve only metro IT staff
MGNREGA bans crop marketing
e: MGNREGA serves as an immediate wage safety net creating rural assets, whereas cold storages, dal mills, and rural credit generate durable year-round employment.

q: Which scenario described in NCERT illustrates workers being forced from the Organised Sector into the Unorganised Sector?
o: Since the 1990s, closure of several organised units and informal hiring compelled many previously formal workers to take low-paid, insecure unorganised jobs
Millions of casual labourers became permanent civil servants
Overtime wages tripled across all small shops
All farmers received monthly corporate pensions
e: Since the 1990s, many organised sector enterprises closed down and workers lost formal jobs, forcing many into low-paying unorganised sector work.

q: A student argues: "Passing a Minimum Wages law alone solves all problems in the unorganised sector; cheap credit or storage facilities are unnecessary." What is the key flaw here?
o: The unorganised sector also includes self-employed rural small/marginal farmers (80% of rural households) and artisans who need timely seeds, cheap credit, storage, and fair markets rather than wage rules alone
Minimum wage laws apply exclusively to pilots
Villages have no artisans or small farmers
Cold storage destroys agricultural produce
e: Because the unorganised sector also encompasses self-employed marginal farmers and small-scale workshops, supporting them requires cheap credit, inputs, storage, and market access alongside wage protections.

q: Why does the government sell foodgrains via PDS or supply electricity to small industries at prices below cost, unlike private corporations?
o: Because the Public Sector is guided by social welfare—protecting food security of poor consumers, supporting farmers, and keeping small industries viable rather than profit alone
Because government lacks accounting departments
Because private firms are legally banned from power plants
Because consumers refuse to use electricity
e: Government raises resources through taxes to bear part of these costs so poor households stay food-secure and small producers remain competitive.

q: A private workshop registers 12 staff under the Factories Act, offering PF, paid leave, and overtime pay. Meanwhile, a government office hires daily-wage cleaners informally with no leave or PF. Classify both:
o: Workshop: Private & Organised Sector; Informal daily-wage cleaners: working under Unorganised conditions even within a Public institution
Both belong strictly to the Unorganised Sector
The workshop is Public Sector
The casual cleaners are in the Organised Sector
e: Organised vs Unorganised depends on terms of employment and statutory protection, whereas Public vs Private depends on ownership.

q: Which sector provides greater job security and benefits, yet employs a much smaller share of India’s workforce compared to the other?
o: The Organised Sector provides better security and benefits, while the vast majority of India’s workforce remains in the Unorganised Sector
The Unorganised Sector provides full pensions and paid leave
95% of Indian workers are in the Organised Sector
Both offer identical legal protection
e: Because employment opportunities in the Organised Sector have expanded slowly, a very large proportion of Indian workers remain in the Unorganised Sector.

q: Even if a mineral-rich backward region has high natural extraction output, why does human development stagnate without Public Sector intervention?
o: Because private profit-driven firms rarely invest in social infrastructure in poor/remote areas; hence government must take care of the poorest and most ignored regions through public investment
Because mining automatically builds universal healthcare
Because residents refuse schools
Because roads are prohibited in plateaus
e: NCERT notes it is the duty of the government to take care of the poorest and most ignored regions through increased public spending in health, education, and housing.

q: Which service from the Tertiary Sector became newly important specifically due to recent Information and Communication Technology (ICT) advances cited in NCERT?
o: Internet cafes, ATM booths, call centres, and software companies
Only post offices and police stations
Pottery and handloom weaving
Traditional bullock-cart transport
e: Over the past decade or so, certain new services based on ICT—such as internet cafes, ATM booths, call centres, and software companies—have become essential in India.

q: How does public investment in school education (human development) directly impact employment challenges in Sectors of the Indian Economy?
o: Expanding education builds skilled human capital enabling surplus farm youth to move into productive manufacturing/services, while schools themselves create ~20 lakh jobs
Higher schooling shuts down factories
Education worsens disguised unemployment
There is no relationship between schooling and sectoral jobs
e: Expanding education directly generates ~20 lakh jobs in schools and equips rural youth to transition out of disguised farm employment into skilled jobs.

q: An economist studies why rural marginal farmers and urban tiny workshops rely heavily on high-interest moneylenders. How does this connect Sectors of Economy with rural credit?
o: Both rural marginal farmers and urban small-scale workshops in the unorganised sector lack affordable credit and inputs, trapping them in low returns without government/bank support
Moneylenders charge 0% interest
Small farmers belong to the organised corporate sector
Banks are barred from lending to agriculture
e: Both small farmers and small-scale workshops in the unorganised sector need affordable formal credit and government backing for inputs and marketing.

q: Synthesising "Development" and "Sectors of the Indian Economy", what emerges as the most balanced development strategy for India?
o: Combining economic growth with shifting surplus farm labour into productive secondary/tertiary jobs, protecting unorganised workers, and investing strongly in public health, education, and environmental sustainability
Building IT parks in one city while neglecting rural schools and healthcare
Maximising short-term GDP by exhausting aquifers and forests
Abolishing all public facilities and welfare schemes
e: True development integrates productive employment shifts across sectors, protections for unorganised workers, equitable public facilities in health/education, and environmental sustainability.
